items.stem:
Read the following speech by a 14-year-old to a regional youth climate conference in Fiji.

Bula, everyone. My name is Losana, and my island is disappearing.
Not in a hundred years. Now. Last year, the sea came into my grandmother's kitchen. Twice.
Some people say: you are just a child, what can you do? I say: I am a child, and that is exactly why I am here. Because it is my future you are spending.
So I ask you three things: listen to islands, cut emissions, and fund the walls that keep the sea out of kitchens.
Vinaka vakalevu – thank you.

Explain how the opening and ending of the speech are designed to affect the audience.
items.answer: Hook: a shocking personal statement ("my island is disappearing"). Argument: the evidence of the sea in her grandmother's kitchen, a counterargument ("you are just a child") and rebuttal. Conclusion: three clear demands and a polite thank-you in Fijian.
items.markingKey: Hook: a shocking personal statement ("my island is disappearing"). Argument: the evidence of the sea in her grandmother's kitchen, a counterargument ("you are just a child") and rebuttal. Conclusion: three clear demands and a polite thank-you in Fijian. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an essay and a speech.
items.answer: A speech is written for listeners, using direct address, repetition, signposting and a strong ending; an essay is written to be read, using paragraphs, formal analysis and references.
items.markingKey: A speech is written for listeners, using direct address, repetition, signposting and a strong ending; an essay is written to be read, using paragraphs, formal analysis and references. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Elena writes: "A speech is just an essay read aloud." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Speeches are designed for the ear: shorter sentences, repetition, direct address and signposting help listeners follow.

items.markingKey: Any effective hook (question, statistic, anecdote), e.g. "Every night, 40 dogs in our city fall asleep waiting for someone who never comes." Credit engagement and relevance.

items.stem:
Read the following acceptance speech by a student winning a school writing award.

Thank you. I genuinely did not prepare this, because I genuinely did not think I would win. (Laughter.)
Two years ago, Ms Ferreira handed back my first story with one comment: 'More you, please.' I didn't understand. I thought stories had to sound like books.
This story is about my little brother, our noisy flat and the day he lost his first tooth in a mango. It is the most 'me' thing I have ever written.
So thank you, Ms Ferreira. And thank you, mango.

Comment on the writer's choice of language in "I genuinely did not prepare this, because I genuinely did not think I would win".
items.answer: Self-deprecating humour: "I genuinely did not prepare this, because I genuinely did not think I would win" – the modest joke wins the audience over immediately.

items.stem:
Read the following transcript of the question-and-answer session after a student talk on food waste.

SPEAKER (Hana, 13): ...so one third of all food produced is wasted. Any questions?
STUDENT 1: Yeah, but what can we actually do?
HANA: Good question! Plan meals, use leftovers, and our canteen could donate unsold food.
STUDENT 2: You said 'one third'. Where is that number from?
HANA: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization. I should have said that – thank you.
STUDENT 3: I disagree. Isn't the real problem supermarkets, not families?
HANA: Both matter. Supermarkets waste a lot, but in many countries households waste even more.

Explain how the speaker responds to each question and what this shows about good listening.
items.answer: Student 1 asks a practical, open question about solutions; Student 2 asks a source/evidence question, which tests the reliability of the statistic; Student 3 challenges the argument respectfully with a counterpoint, which pushes the speaker to give a balanced answer.
items.markingKey: Student 1 asks a practical, open question about solutions; Student 2 asks a source/evidence question, which tests the reliability of the statistic; Student 3 challenges the argument respectfully with a counterpoint, which pushes the speaker to give a balanced answer. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

Read the following speech by a student council president to her school assembly in Toronto.

Good morning, everyone. Raise your hand if you checked your phone before breakfast today. (Pause.) Me too.
We are the most connected generation in history – and, according to our own school survey, 62 per cent of us say we feel lonely every week. Connected, but alone.
I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake. I'm asking for one hour. One lunchtime a week, phones in our bags, eyes on each other.
Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

items.stem: "Questioning a speaker is rude." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Respectful questions show engagement and help test and develop ideas; tone and wording keep them polite.

items.stem:
Read the following acceptance speech by a student winning a school writing award.

Thank you. I genuinely did not prepare this, because I genuinely did not think I would win. (Laughter.)
Two years ago, Ms Ferreira handed back my first story with one comment: 'More you, please.' I didn't understand. I thought stories had to sound like books.
This story is about my little brother, our noisy flat and the day he lost his first tooth in a mango. It is the most 'me' thing I have ever written.
So thank you, Ms Ferreira. And thank you, mango.

Identify the hook, the main argument and the conclusion of this speech and explain how each works.
items.answer: Hook: humorous honesty that he did not prepare. Body: an anecdote about a teacher's comment and what the story is about. Conclusion: thanks to the teacher and a comic callback ("thank you, mango").
items.markingKey: Hook: humorous honesty that he did not prepare. Body: an anecdote about a teacher's comment and what the story is about. Conclusion: thanks to the teacher and a comic callback ("thank you, mango"). Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

Read the following speech by a student council president to her school assembly in Toronto.

Good morning, everyone. Raise your hand if you checked your phone before breakfast today. (Pause.) Me too.
We are the most connected generation in history – and, according to our own school survey, 62 per cent of us say we feel lonely every week. Connected, but alone.
I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake. I'm asking for one hour. One lunchtime a week, phones in our bags, eyes on each other.
Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

How would you describe the writer's tone? Refer to two language choices that create it.
items.answer: The tone is warm and persuasive: humour, inclusive pronouns and a modest request create a warm tone.

items.stem:
Read the following transcript of the question-and-answer session after a student talk on food waste.

SPEAKER (Hana, 13): ...so one third of all food produced is wasted. Any questions?
STUDENT 1: Yeah, but what can we actually do?
HANA: Good question! Plan meals, use leftovers, and our canteen could donate unsold food.
STUDENT 2: You said 'one third'. Where is that number from?
HANA: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization. I should have said that – thank you.
STUDENT 3: I disagree. Isn't the real problem supermarkets, not families?
HANA: Both matter. Supermarkets waste a lot, but in many countries households waste even more.

Analyse the questions the listeners ask in this transcript: what does each type of question achieve?
items.answer: Student 1 asks a practical, open question about solutions; Student 2 asks a source/evidence question, which tests the reliability of the statistic; Student 3 challenges the argument respectfully with a counterpoint, which pushes the speaker to give a balanced answer.
items.markingKey: Student 1 asks a practical, open question about solutions; Student 2 asks a source/evidence question, which tests the reliability of the statistic; Student 3 challenges the argument respectfully with a counterpoint, which pushes the speaker to give a balanced answer. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Distinguish between a speech and an essay.
items.answer: A speech is written for listeners, using direct address, repetition, signposting and a strong ending; an essay is written to be read, using paragraphs, formal analysis and references.
items.markingKey: A speech is written for listeners, using direct address, repetition, signposting and a strong ending; an essay is written to be read, using paragraphs, formal analysis and references. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a 14-year-old to a regional youth climate conference in Fiji.

Bula, everyone. My name is Losana, and my island is disappearing.
Not in a hundred years. Now. Last year, the sea came into my grandmother's kitchen. Twice.
Some people say: you are just a child, what can you do? I say: I am a child, and that is exactly why I am here. Because it is my future you are spending.
So I ask you three things: listen to islands, cut emissions, and fund the walls that keep the sea out of kitchens.
Vinaka vakalevu – thank you.

Explain how a speaker could use pauses and emphasis to make "Some people say: you are just a child ... I say: I am a child, and that is exactly why I am here." more powerful.
items.answer: Counterargument and rebuttal: "Some people say: you are just a child ... I say: I am a child, and that is exactly why I am here." – she turns a criticism into her strongest argument.
items.markingKey: Counterargument and rebuttal: "Some people say: you are just a child ... I say: I am a child, and that is exactly why I am here." – she turns a criticism into her strongest argument. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student council president to her school assembly in Toronto.

Good morning, everyone. Raise your hand if you checked your phone before breakfast today. (Pause.) Me too.
We are the most connected generation in history – and, according to our own school survey, 62 per cent of us say we feel lonely every week. Connected, but alone.
I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake. I'm asking for one hour. One lunchtime a week, phones in our bags, eyes on each other.
Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

How does the speaker persuade her audience to try a phone-free lunchtime?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The speaker builds trust before persuading: the opening show of hands and "Me too" make the habit shared, not shameful (ethos). The school statistic and the paradox "Connected, but alone" give logical and emotional weight. The humorous concession shrinks the request to "one hour", and the anaphoric "Let's..." ending turns agreement into collective action, closing on the emotive image of friends laughing.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The speaker builds trust before persuading: the opening show of hands and "Me too" make the habit shared, not shameful (ethos). The school statistic and the paradox "Connected, but alone" give logical and emotional weight. The humorous concession shrinks the request to "one hour", and the anaphoric "Let's..." ending turns agreement into collective action, closing on the emotive image of friends laughing. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: "How a speech is delivered matters more than what it says." Discuss.
items.answer: Delivery and content work together: great delivery cannot save weak ideas for long, and strong ideas need effective delivery to be heard.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: poor delivery loses the audience; confident delivery persuades. Arguments against: strong content gives the speech substance; audiences notice empty rhetoric. Supported judgement: Delivery and content work together: great delivery cannot save weak ideas for long, and strong ideas need effective delivery to be heard. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.
